title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 168
paragraphs: So much for affairs in Sicily. As for the Corcyreans, they answered the envoys as follows — and then acted as I shall now relate. The same men who had gone to Sicily tried to enlist the Corcyreans' help too, using the same arguments they had used with Gelon; and the Corcyreans at the time promised to send a force and to help in the defense, declaring that they must not permit Greece to be ruined without an effort on their part, for if it suffered disaster they would themselves be reduced to subjection from the very first day, and they must give aid to the utmost of their power. Thus speciously they replied; but when the time came to send help, they manned sixty ships, having other intentions in mind, and after much delay finally put out to sea and reached the Peloponnese. Then near Pylos and Taenarum in the Lacedaemonian territory they kept their ships at anchor, waiting, like Gelon, to see how the war would turn out; for they did not expect the Greeks to prevail but thought the Persian would easily get the better of them and be ruler of all Greece. They were acting deliberately in order to be able to say to the Persian something like this: “O king, when the Greeks tried to get our help in this war, we, who possess a not inconsiderable force, and could have supplied a ship contingent second only to the Athenians, refused to oppose you or to do anything contrary to your wish.” By such a speech they hoped to gain some advantage over the others, and so, I believe, it would have turned out. Meanwhile they had an excuse ready-made for the Greeks too, which is the one they actually used: when the Greeks reproached them for not coming to help, they said they had manned sixty triremes but had been unable to get past Cape Malea because of the Etesian winds; that was why they had not come to Salamis — not from any want of courage on their part that they had missed the sea-fight.
